JPG is better when you only need compatibility and want the smallest possible file size.

heic-to-png.q: Will HEIC to PNG conversion preserve transparency?
heic-to-png.a: Standard iPhone HEIC photos do not contain transparency — they are fully opaque images. The HEIC to PNG converter will produce a fully opaque PNG from a standard iPhone photo. If you specifically need a transparent cutout, use the Background Remover tool on the converted PNG to isolate the subject after conversion.

heic-to-png.q: How large will the PNG file be compared to the original HEIC?
heic-to-png.a: PNG files from HEIC conversion are significantly larger than the HEIC source because PNG is lossless and HEIC is an extremely efficient lossy codec. A 3 MB HEIC iPhone photo may produce a 10–20 MB PNG. If file size is a concern, convert to JPG at quality 90 instead, which produces a file roughly similar in size to the original HEIC while maintaining excellent quality.

heic-to-png.q: Is the conversion private? Are my photos uploaded to a server?
heic-to-png.a: All processing is local. The HEIC file is read from your device, decoded in browser memory using a WebAssembly HEIC decoder, and re-encoded as PNG — no data leaves your machine at any point. This is critical for iPhone photos that contain personal EXIF metadata, GPS locations, and facial recognition information.

heic-to-png.q: Can I convert HEIC portrait mode or HDR photos to PNG?
heic-to-png.a: Yes — the converter handles standard HEIC captures including portrait mode photos with depth information (though the depth map data is discarded in the PNG output, leaving only the final composited image). HDR HEIC photos are tone-mapped to standard dynamic range during conversion since PNG does not support HDR output without special extensions.

avif-to-jpg.q: What is AVIF and why would I need to convert it to JPG?
avif-to-jpg.a: AVIF (AV1 Image File Format) is a next-generation image format developed by the Alliance for Open Media that offers significantly better compression than JPG and PNG. While modern browsers support AVIF, most desktop applications, email clients, print services, and operating systems do not yet have native AVIF decoders. Converting AVIF to JPG makes the image accessible in any application or workflow without requiring special codec installation.

avif-to-jpg.q: Does converting AVIF to JPG reduce image quality?
avif-to-jpg.a: The AVIF source may already use lossy compression, and JPG adds another layer of lossy compression during conversion. At JPG quality 90 or above, additional quality loss is minimal on photographic content. AVIF files sometimes use 10-bit color depth, which gets downsampled to 8-bit JPG — this can cause subtle banding in smooth gradients at lower quality settings.

avif-to-jpg.q: How does AVIF compare to JPG in terms of compression?
avif-to-jpg.a: AVIF typically achieves 50% smaller file sizes than JPG at comparable visual quality, making it the most efficient image format currently in widespread use. JPG remains relevant because of its universal compatibility — virtually every device, application, and platform supports JPG, while AVIF requires modern software. Converting AVIF to JPG trades superior compression for universal accessibility.

avif-to-jpg.q: Is AVIF to JPG conversion done privately without server uploads?
avif-to-jpg.a: Yes — the entire conversion is local. The tool uses a WebAssembly-compiled AVIF decoder based on the libaom library to decode the AVIF file in browser memory, then re-encodes the pixel data as JPG using a JavaScript JPEG encoder. No part of your image is transmitted over the network.

avif-to-jpg.q: Can this tool handle all types of AVIF files?
avif-to-jpg.a: The converter handles standard AVIF still images, including those with 8-bit and 10-bit color depth and those with or without an alpha channel. Animated AVIF (AAVIF) files are not fully supported — the converter will extract the first frame of an animated AVIF as a static JPG. Very high-bit-depth HDR AVIF files are tone-mapped to standard dynamic range during JPG output.

avif-to-png.q: Why would I convert AVIF to PNG instead of JPG?
avif-to-png.a: Choose PNG when the AVIF source contains transparency that must be preserved in the output — PNG's alpha channel handles this correctly while JPG does not. PNG is also preferred when the converted image will undergo further editing, since lossless encoding prevents any additional quality degradation from the conversion itself. JPG is the better choice when file size and compatibility are the only goals and transparency is not needed.

avif-to-png.q: Does AVIF to PNG conversion preserve the full AVIF quality?
avif-to-png.a: If the source AVIF used lossy compression, converting to PNG will preserve the pixel data as-is without introducing further loss — but it cannot restore detail that was already discarded by the AVIF encoder. Lossless AVIF sources convert to PNG with perfect pixel-for-pixel fidelity. In both cases, the PNG output is the best lossless representation of the AVIF's current pixel state.

avif-to-png.q: Are my AVIF files uploaded during conversion?
avif-to-png.a: No. AVIF decoding and PNG encoding both happen entirely in your browser using WebAssembly libraries. Your AVIF files — whether downloaded from websites, received from modern cameras, or exported from design tools — stay on your device throughout the entire process. The converted PNG is made available for download without any network transmission.

avif-to-png.q: How does the PNG file size compare to the original AVIF?
avif-to-png.a: PNG files are substantially larger than AVIF because AVIF's compression is far more efficient than PNG's lossless algorithm. A 100 KB AVIF might expand to 1–3 MB as PNG, depending on image complexity and dimensions. This size increase is the expected cost of achieving universal lossless compatibility — consider it a storage cost for editability and broad software support.

avif-to-png.q: Can I convert AVIF with transparency to PNG?
avif-to-png.a: Yes — AVIF supports an alpha channel, and the converter correctly maps AVIF transparency to the PNG alpha channel in the output. The resulting PNG will display transparent areas correctly in any application or browser that supports PNG transparency. This makes AVIF to PNG the correct conversion path for icons, logos, and graphic assets that require transparency.

svg-to-png.q: What resolution should I set when converting SVG to PNG?
svg-to-png.a: Set the output resolution based on your largest intended use case. For web display at 200×200 CSS pixels on retina screens, export at 400×400 PNG and scale down with CSS. For app icons, export at the largest required size (1024×1024) and scale down for smaller variants. For print at 300 DPI, multiply your physical inch dimensions by 300 to get the required pixel dimensions.

svg-to-png.q: Why does my SVG look different after converting to PNG?
svg-to-png.a: SVG rendering relies on fonts, external resources, and CSS that the conversion tool may not have access to. If your SVG references external font files, web fonts via @import, or linked images rather than embedding them, the converted PNG may show fallback fonts or missing elements. Ensure all resources are embedded directly in the SVG file before conversion to guarantee accurate rasterization.

svg-to-png.q: Does SVG to PNG conversion support transparency?
svg-to-png.a: Yes — if your SVG has a transparent background (no background rectangle fill), the resulting PNG will correctly have a transparent background with the alpha channel preserving the SVG's clear areas. This is one of the key advantages of PNG output over JPG for SVG-sourced content, since most vector illustrations and icons expect to be placed on various background colors.

svg-to-png.q: Is my SVG file processed on a server?
svg-to-png.a: No. SVG rendering and PNG conversion happen entirely in the browser using the browser's native SVG rendering engine and the HTML5 Canvas API. The SVG is drawn to an off-screen canvas at your specified dimensions and exported as a PNG Blob — no server request is made at any point. Your SVG source code, including any embedded proprietary illustrations, remains local.

svg-to-png.q: Can I convert animated SVGs to PNG?
svg-to-png.a: The SVG to PNG converter captures a static snapshot of the SVG at the initial state, which means animated SVG elements (SMIL animations or CSS animations) will be frozen at their starting position in the output PNG. If you need to capture a specific animation frame, pause the animation at that frame in a browser and use a screenshot approach, or use the Video to GIF tool for motion content.

svg-to-jpg.q: When should I use SVG to JPG instead of SVG to PNG?
svg-to-jpg.a: Choose JPG over PNG when the converted image will be used as a photograph-like flat image where file size matters more than transparency — such as Open Graph social preview images, email header graphics, or compressed web backgrounds. Choose PNG when the SVG has a transparent background that must be preserved or when the image will be edited further. For logos and icons, PNG is almost always the better choice.

svg-to-jpg.q: What background color will transparent SVG areas get in the JPG output?
svg-to-jpg.a: Transparent areas in the SVG will be filled with white by default during JPG conversion, since JPG has no alpha channel. The converter lets you specify a custom background fill color before converting — set it to match the page background color of your website or document to ensure the SVG appears seamless in context. Failure to set the correct background color results in white boxes where transparency was expected.

svg-to-jpg.q: Does SVG to JPG conversion handle complex SVG features like filters and masks?
svg-to-jpg.a: The converter uses the browser's native SVG rendering engine, which supports the vast majority of SVG 1.1 features including filters (blur, drop shadow), masks, clipping paths, gradients, and patterns. Very cutting-edge SVG 2.0 features or non-standard extensions may not render as expected. Test the output visually against the original SVG before using in production.

svg-to-jpg.q: Is the SVG source code uploaded during conversion?
svg-to-jpg.a: No. The SVG is rendered locally by the browser's built-in SVG renderer onto an HTML5 Canvas element, then exported as a JPG using the Canvas toBlob API. The SVG file content never leaves your device. This protects any proprietary artwork, custom iconography, or confidential diagrams embedded in the SVG.

svg-to-jpg.q: Why is my JPG from SVG showing compression artifacts on sharp edges?
svg-to-jpg.a: JPG's compression algorithm is optimized for photographic gradients and performs poorly on the sharp edges, thin lines, and solid color transitions typical of vector-sourced artwork. Increase the quality setting to 92 or above to minimize ringing artifacts on text and geometric shapes. If sharp edges are critical, use SVG to PNG instead, since PNG's lossless compression preserves vector-source sharpness perfectly.

compress-image.q: What quality setting should I use for web images?
compress-image.a: For photographic images (JPG, WebP), a quality setting of 80–85 provides the optimal balance between visual quality and file size for web use — most viewers cannot distinguish these from higher-quality originals at normal screen sizes. For UI screenshots and images with text or sharp edges, use 85–90 to avoid visible compression artifacts on fine details. PNG lossless compression mode is recommended for graphics, icons, and diagrams regardless of quality setting.

compress-image.q: How much can image compression reduce my file sizes?
compress-image.a: Results vary significantly by image content and source quality, but photographic JPG images compressed from quality 100 to quality 85 typically see 60–75% file size reduction. PNG images optimized with lossless compression can see 10–40% reduction depending on the original optimizer used. Overall, most unoptimized images from cameras and design exports can be reduced by 50–80% with no perceptible quality loss.

compress-image.q: Does compressing an image permanently damage the original?
compress-image.a: This tool creates a new compressed file — it does not overwrite your original. Always keep your original high-resolution files archived and use compressed versions for web and sharing. For JPG images, each re-compression at a lower quality setting does degrade quality slightly, so it's best practice to compress once from the highest-quality source rather than re-compressing an already compressed image.

compress-image.q: Are my images uploaded to a server for compression?
compress-image.a: No. Image compression is performed entirely in your browser. JPG compression uses a JavaScript JPEG encoder, PNG optimization uses WebAssembly-compiled pngquant or zopfli, and WebP compression uses the WebAssembly libwebp library — all running locally on your device. Your images, including any sensitive personal or business content, are never transmitted to any server.

compress-image.q: Can I compress PNG images without reducing quality?
compress-image.a: Yes — PNG supports lossless compression, meaning you can reduce PNG file size by recompressing with a better algorithm without changing a single pixel. The lossless compression mode in this tool applies stronger compression passes (equivalent to pngquant/zopfli) that many image editors skip for speed. Typical lossless PNG savings are 10–40% over default-exported PNGs from Photoshop or design tools.

remove-bg.q: How accurate is the AI background removal?
remove-bg.a: The AI segmentation model performs excellently on images with clear subject-background contrast — product photos on solid backgrounds, people against simple outdoor scenes, and animals on distinct surfaces. Accuracy decreases on images with complex backgrounds similar in color to the subject, fine hair or fur details, transparent or reflective objects, and scenes with multiple overlapping subjects. For challenging cases, use a professional tool with manual refinement controls.

remove-bg.q: What image formats does the background remover output?
remove-bg.a: The background remover always outputs a PNG file with a transparent alpha channel representing the removed background areas. PNG is the only widely supported format with full alpha-channel transparency, making it the universal output for cutout images. You can then convert the transparent PNG to a different format with a custom background color if needed using the other conversion tools.

remove-bg.q: Is my photo uploaded to an AI server for processing?
remove-bg.a: No — the AI segmentation model is downloaded to your browser and runs locally using WebAssembly and WebGL acceleration. Your images are processed entirely on your device; no photo data is transmitted to any server at any point. This is particularly important for portrait photos, medical images, and proprietary product photography that must remain private.

remove-bg.q: How do I get the best results from background removal?
remove-bg.a: Photograph your subject against a high-contrast background — a bright white sheet, a solid-colored wall, or a clearly distinct outdoor setting. Ensure good, even lighting with no harsh shadows that cross the subject boundary. Avoid subjects wearing clothing that closely matches the background color. Sharp focus on the subject's edges significantly improves AI segmentation accuracy.

remove-bg.q: Can the background remover handle hair, fur, and fine details?
remove-bg.a: Modern AI segmentation handles hair and fur much better than legacy chroma-key or edge-detection methods, but very fine, wispy hair against complex backgrounds remains challenging and may require manual touch-up. For best hair results, photograph against a plain light-colored background with backlight separating hair from the background. The AI performs best when there is strong luminance contrast at the subject edge.

resize-image.q: Does resizing an image reduce its quality?
resize-image.a: Downscaling (making an image smaller) generally maintains or improves perceived sharpness because the resampling algorithm averages pixel data to create a denser image. Upscaling (making an image larger) always reduces quality — the algorithm must interpolate pixel data that does not exist, resulting in blurriness or pixelation. Use a high-quality source image at the largest needed size and scale down, never up, for best results.

resize-image.q: What resampling algorithm does the image resizer use?
resize-image.a: The resizer uses Lanczos3 resampling for downscaling — the same algorithm used by Photoshop's 'Bicubic Sharper' mode — which produces the sharpest, cleanest results with minimal aliasing. For upscaling, bilinear interpolation is used, which produces smooth results without the ringing artifacts of Lanczos upscaling. Both algorithms run in WebAssembly for native performance speed.

resize-image.q: Can I resize images while keeping the aspect ratio?
resize-image.a: Yes — enabling the 'lock aspect ratio' option ensures that when you change width or height, the other dimension is automatically calculated to maintain the original proportions. This prevents stretching or squishing distortion. Disable aspect ratio lock only when you intentionally need non-proportional resizing, such as fitting an image to a fixed-dimension slot in a layout.

resize-image.q: Are my images uploaded to a server when I resize them?
resize-image.a: No. The image resizer uses the HTML5 Canvas API and WebAssembly pixel processing entirely within your browser. Full-resolution photos, which may contain EXIF metadata including GPS location and timestamp, are resized locally and never transmitted to any server. The resized output file is generated in browser memory and downloaded directly to your device.

resize-image.q: What is the maximum image size I can resize?
resize-image.a: The practical limit is determined by your device's available browser memory rather than a hard restriction. Most modern computers can resize images up to 50–100 megapixels (e.g., a 10,000×10,000 pixel image) without issues. Very large images — such as those from high-resolution scanners or gigapixel cameras — may require more memory than lower-end devices provide; if the browser becomes unresponsive, resize the image in smaller steps.

crop-image.q: Does cropping an image reduce quality?
crop-image.a: Cropping itself does not reduce image quality — it simply removes pixels outside the selected region and outputs the remaining area at full original quality. The cropped output maintains the same resolution and quality as the source within the crop boundary. Quality is only reduced if you subsequently resize the cropped area to a size larger than the pixels available in the crop region.

crop-image.q: Can I crop to specific aspect ratios like 16:9 or 1:1?
crop-image.a: Yes — the cropper offers preset aspect ratios including 1:1 (square), 16:9 (widescreen), 4:3 (standard), 3:2 (photo print), and 9:16 (portrait/Stories). Select a preset to constrain the crop handle to that ratio, then drag and reposition the crop box to frame your subject. Custom aspect ratios can be set by entering width and height values manually.

crop-image.q: What formats does the image cropper support?
crop-image.a: The cropper accepts JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, and most common raster image formats. The output format matches the input format by default — cropping a PNG outputs a PNG, cropping a JPG outputs a JPG. If you need to change format during cropping, use the format selector before downloading to convert and crop in a single step.

crop-image.q: Is my image uploaded to a server for cropping?
crop-image.a: No. The image is loaded into an HTML5 Canvas element in your browser, the crop region is selected visually using the browser's rendering engine, and the cropped output is generated locally using the Canvas API. No image data is transmitted to any server at any stage. Sensitive images — ID documents, medical scans, proprietary designs — can be cropped with full privacy.

crop-image.q: Can I undo a crop or try different crop regions before downloading?
crop-image.a: Yes — the crop tool has a non-destructive preview workflow where you adjust the crop selection as many times as needed before clicking the download button. The original image remains unchanged in memory until you export. If you download and then want a different crop, simply reload the original file into the tool and create a new selection.

rotate-image.q: Will rotating a JPG reduce its quality?
rotate-image.a: Rotating a JPG by exactly 90°, 180°, or 270° can technically be done losslessly at the JPEG block level (known as lossless JPEG rotation), but browser-based canvas rotation re-encodes the image at a high quality setting, introducing minimal additional compression. For PNG, BMP, and other lossless source formats, rotation is always lossless since re-encoding the output as PNG introduces no quality penalty.

rotate-image.q: Can I rotate an image by an arbitrary angle, like 15 degrees?
rotate-image.a: Yes — the tool supports free-angle rotation in addition to the standard 90°/180°/270° presets. When rotating by a non-right angle, the output image dimensions expand to fit the rotated content, and corner areas outside the original image are filled with a background color (white by default, or transparent for PNG output). Note that arbitrary-angle rotation always requires a full re-encode and introduces slight quality reduction in JPG output.

rotate-image.q: What is the difference between rotate and flip?
rotate-image.a: Rotation changes the orientation by turning the image around its center point (90°, 180°, etc.). Flipping mirrors the image across an axis — horizontal flip mirrors left-to-right (as if reflecting in a vertical mirror), and vertical flip mirrors top-to-bottom. Both operations are available in the tool. Flipping is useful for correcting mirrored text in screenshots and creating symmetrical compositions.

rotate-image.q: Are my images uploaded to rotate them?
rotate-image.a: No. Image rotation uses the HTML5 Canvas API to draw the source image at the specified rotation angle and export the result — all within your browser's memory without any server communication. This is particularly relevant for photos containing embedded EXIF location data or personal information that should remain private.

rotate-image.q: Why does my image already appear rotated correctly on my phone but sideways when I upload it?
rotate-image.a: Camera apps save JPG photos with an EXIF orientation tag indicating which direction is 'up,' and most image viewers on phones automatically apply this rotation. However, many web applications, CMSes, and design tools ignore EXIF orientation metadata and display the raw pixel data — which may be sideways or upside down. Using the rotate tool to physically rotate the pixels and re-save the image removes the dependency on EXIF metadata for correct display.

image-filter.q: Are the filter adjustments destructive or non-destructive?
image-filter.a: Adjustments are applied non-destructively in the preview — you can freely adjust any slider and see the result in real time without altering the original image data. The filters are only baked into the pixel data when you export and download the result. If you want to try a different look, simply reset the sliders and the original image is fully restored in the preview.

image-filter.q: What filters and adjustments are available?
image-filter.a: The tool includes brightness, contrast, saturation, hue rotation, sharpness, blur (Gaussian), grayscale, sepia tone, vignette, invert, and temperature/tint adjustments. Multiple filters can be combined and are applied in a defined order to the image. The filter stack is reset on each new export, so the original file is always the source regardless of how many adjustments you make in a session.

image-filter.q: Does applying filters reduce image quality?
image-filter.a: The filter adjustments themselves are calculated at full floating-point precision in the canvas pixel buffer. The only quality reduction occurs at export when the result is re-encoded as JPG (lossy) or PNG (lossless). For JPG output, use a quality setting of 90 or above to minimize export compression artifacts, especially on images with sharpening applied, which amplifies existing JPEG noise.

image-filter.q: Is my photo processed on a server when I apply filters?
image-filter.a: No. All filter processing uses CSS filter operations and HTML5 Canvas pixel manipulation that execute entirely within your browser's GPU and CPU rendering pipeline. Your images — including personal portraits and confidential business graphics — are never transmitted to any external server for processing.

image-filter.q: Can I save a filter preset to reuse the same look on multiple images?
image-filter.a: The tool supports named presets that save your current slider configuration for reuse across different images in the same session. Presets are stored in browser localStorage so they persist between browser sessions on the same device. For batch applying the same filter settings to multiple images, use the Batch Image Processor tool, which accepts filter presets as part of the processing pipeline.

add-watermark.q: Can a watermark be removed from my images?
add-watermark.a: A well-placed watermark significantly increases the effort required to remove it, deterring casual theft. A corner watermark is relatively easy to crop away; a tiled or centered watermark over the subject is much harder to remove without visibly damaging the image. For the strongest protection, use a semi-transparent tiled watermark at 20–30% opacity that covers the entire image — AI inpainting tools can still attempt removal, but the effort deters most unauthorized use.

add-watermark.q: Can I watermark multiple images at once?
add-watermark.a: For single images, use this dedicated watermark tool for the best positioning and preview experience. For watermarking many images with the same settings, use the Batch Image Processor, which supports watermark overlays as part of the batch processing pipeline. Both tools apply the watermark locally in the browser without uploading your images.

add-watermark.q: What types of watermarks can I add?
add-watermark.a: The tool supports both text watermarks (custom text, font, size, color, opacity, rotation) and image watermarks (upload a logo PNG with transparency). Text watermarks can be positioned at preset locations (corners, center, tiled) or placed with custom coordinates. Image watermarks maintain the transparency of the source PNG, making them ideal for logo overlays that blend naturally with the photo.

add-watermark.q: Are my images uploaded to a server when adding a watermark?
add-watermark.a: No — the watermark is composited entirely in the browser using the HTML5 Canvas API. Your source images and the watermark graphic are drawn together on an off-screen canvas, and the merged result is exported locally for download. Neither your photos nor your logo or brand assets are transmitted over the network.

add-watermark.q: What opacity should I use for a watermark?
add-watermark.a: For deterrence with minimal visual intrusion on a portfolio or preview site, 20–30% opacity is the standard range — visible enough to identify and deter theft, subtle enough not to obscure the work itself. For explicit copyright marking on sample images sent to clients, 40–60% opacity is more appropriate since legibility matters more than aesthetics. Avoid opacity below 15% as the watermark becomes too easy to overlook or remove.

drawing-canvas.q: Is the drawing canvas suitable for professional illustration work?
drawing-canvas.a: The drawing canvas is optimized for quick sketches, annotations, diagrams, and lightweight creative tasks rather than professional illustration. It lacks layer support, advanced brush engines, vector drawing, and the pressure-sensitivity features of professional tools like Procreate or Photoshop. For professional illustration, use a dedicated application; for fast annotations, wireframe sketches, and teaching diagrams, the canvas is highly effective.

drawing-canvas.q: Does the drawing canvas support touch and stylus input?
drawing-canvas.a: Yes — the canvas uses the Pointer Events API, which supports mouse, touch, and stylus input on compatible devices. On iPads with Apple Pencil or Android tablets with a stylus, pressure and tilt data from the stylus are used to vary brush size and opacity, providing a more natural drawing feel. On touchscreens without a stylus, finger drawing works but is less precise.

drawing-canvas.q: Will I lose my drawing if I close the browser tab?
drawing-canvas.a: The drawing canvas saves your in-progress work to browser localStorage automatically, so reloading the page or closing and reopening the tab will restore your last drawing session. However, clearing browser data, switching devices, or using private browsing mode will clear the saved state. For important work, export the PNG frequently to ensure you have a saved copy on your device.

drawing-canvas.q: What format does the canvas export in?
drawing-canvas.a: The canvas exports as a PNG file with a transparent background by default (if you have not filled the background with a color), allowing the drawing to be overlaid on any background in a design tool. You can also set a solid background color before exporting if you prefer an opaque image. SVG export is not currently supported — the canvas works with raster pixel data rather than vector paths.

drawing-canvas.q: Can I import an image into the drawing canvas to annotate it?
drawing-canvas.a: Yes — you can drag and drop or upload an existing image as the background layer of the canvas, then draw annotations, arrows, circles, and text on top of it. This is particularly useful for reviewing screenshots, marking up design mockups, or explaining UI issues in support tickets. The exported PNG includes both the background image and all drawn annotations as a flat merged image.

image-batch.q: How many images can I process in a single batch job?
image-batch.a: The batch processor handles up to 100 images per job on most modern devices. The practical limit is determined by total combined file size and available browser memory. For jobs with very large source files (over 10 MB each), process in smaller groups of 20–30 to avoid memory pressure. Each job's progress is shown individually, so you can monitor which files have been processed successfully.

image-batch.q: Can I apply different settings to different images in the same batch?
image-batch.a: No — batch processing applies the same settings uniformly to all images in the job by design. This ensures consistency across the entire set of output files. If you need different settings for different subsets of images, organize them into separate batches with the appropriate settings for each group before processing.

image-batch.q: What operations can I perform in batch mode?
image-batch.a: The batch processor supports format conversion (JPG, PNG, WebP), resize by pixel dimensions or percentage, quality/compression adjustment, and watermark overlay — all configurable before starting the job. Operations can be combined, so you can convert PNG to WebP, resize to 800px wide, and compress to quality 85 in a single pass across all uploaded images.

image-batch.q: Are my images uploaded to a server for batch processing?
image-batch.a: No — batch processing uses Web Workers and WebAssembly to process all images in parallel threads within the browser. Your files never leave your device, which is critical when batch-processing large libraries of personal photos, confidential product images, or proprietary design assets. All output files are bundled into a ZIP archive generated locally and downloaded to your device.

image-batch.q: What output format does batch processing produce?
image-batch.a: Batch-processed images are delivered as a single ZIP archive containing all output files with their original filenames (modified with the new extension if format conversion was applied). The ZIP file is generated in the browser using the JSZip library without any server interaction. You can extract the ZIP and use the output files immediately without any additional steps.

image-to-pdf.q: What image formats can I convert to PDF?
image-to-pdf.a: The tool supports JPG, JPEG, PNG, and WebP images. These cover the vast majority of common image formats produced by cameras, smartphones, and screenshot tools. If you have a different format such as BMP or TIFF, convert it to PNG first using an image editor, then use this tool.

image-to-pdf.q: Are my images uploaded to a server during conversion?
image-to-pdf.a: No. The entire conversion is performed locally in your browser using the pdf-lib JavaScript library. Your images are read from your local disk, processed in memory, and written as a PDF file that is downloaded directly to your device. No image data is ever transmitted over the internet.

image-to-pdf.q: Will the PDF output preserve my image quality?
image-to-pdf.a: Yes. pdf-lib embeds images at their original resolution without additional compression, so the PDF quality is determined entirely by the quality of the source images you provide. For the sharpest results, use high-resolution PNG images rather than heavily compressed JPGs.

image-to-pdf.q: How many images can I combine into one PDF?
image-to-pdf.a: There is no hard limit on the number of images, but performance is constrained by available browser memory. Combining dozens of high-resolution images may slow down the browser on low-memory devices. If you encounter slowness, try working in batches of 20–30 images and then merging the resulting PDFs.

image-to-pdf.q: Can I control the order of pages in the output PDF?
image-to-pdf.a: Yes. After adding images, you can drag and drop them in the list to set the desired page order before converting. The PDF will be generated with pages in exactly the sequence you arrange, giving you full control without needing to re-upload files.

merge-pdf.q: Does merging PDFs affect the quality of the original content?
merge-pdf.a: No. pdf-lib performs a document merge that copies page content streams directly without re-encoding or recompressing anything. Text, images, vector graphics, and embedded fonts from the source PDFs are preserved exactly as they were in the originals.

merge-pdf.q: Are my PDF files uploaded to a server when I merge them?
merge-pdf.a: No. All merging happens entirely within your browser using pdf-lib. Your files are read locally, combined in browser memory, and the resulting merged PDF is downloaded directly to your device without any network transfer of file content.

Not directly. pdf-lib cannot read encrypted PDF content. You must first remove the password from each protected PDF using the PDF Decrypt tool, then merge the unlocked versions. Attempting to merge a still-encrypted PDF will result in an error or garbled output.

merge-pdf.q: Is there a limit to how many PDFs I can merge at once?
merge-pdf.a: There is no enforced file count limit, but the browser's available RAM sets a practical ceiling. Very large PDFs or a high number of files may exhaust browser memory. If merging fails or the browser becomes unresponsive, try merging files in smaller groups and then combining the intermediate results.

merge-pdf.q: Will bookmarks and hyperlinks from the original PDFs be preserved?
merge-pdf.a: Internal hyperlinks within each document are generally preserved, but document-level bookmarks (outlines) from individual files are not automatically merged into a combined outline in the output PDF. If you need a unified bookmark structure, you would need to add those manually using a full PDF editor after merging.

split-pdf.q: How do I specify which pages to extract?
split-pdf.a: You enter page numbers as a comma-separated list, ranges using a dash, or a combination of both — for example, '1,3,5-8,12' extracts pages 1, 3, 5 through 8, and 12. The tool interprets the input and extracts exactly the specified pages into separate output files.

split-pdf.q: Is my PDF sent to a server when I split it?
split-pdf.a: No. PDF splitting is performed entirely in your browser. The file is loaded into browser memory, the requested pages are extracted using pdf-lib, and the output files are downloaded directly to your device. No content is transmitted to any external server.

split-pdf.q: Does splitting reduce the quality of the extracted pages?
split-pdf.a: No. Pages are extracted by copying content streams directly — no recompression or re-encoding occurs. The extracted pages are identical in quality to those in the source PDF, including all embedded fonts, images, and vector graphics.

split-pdf.q: Can I split a password-protected PDF?
split-pdf.a: No. Encrypted PDFs cannot be split directly because the tool cannot access the protected content streams. Use the PDF Decrypt tool first to remove the open password, then split the unlocked PDF.

split-pdf.q: What happens if I enter a page number that exceeds the document's total pages?
split-pdf.a: The tool validates page numbers against the actual page count of the uploaded PDF and will alert you if you specify a page number outside the valid range. Only valid page numbers within the document's range will be included in the output.

pdf-compress.q: How much will compression reduce my PDF file size?
pdf-compress.a: The reduction depends heavily on what the PDF contains. PDFs with large embedded photographs can see 50–80% size reduction, while PDFs containing mostly text and vector graphics may see little to no reduction since those elements are already stored efficiently. Metadata stripping provides a small additional reduction on most files.

pdf-compress.q: Will compression damage the text in my PDF?
pdf-compress.a: No. Text layers and vector graphics are preserved without modification. Only raster images embedded in the PDF are recompressed at a lower quality level. This means the readable content of documents remains sharp while the file size decreases.

pdf-compress.q: Is my PDF uploaded to a server for compression?
pdf-compress.a: No. Compression is performed entirely within the browser. Your file is read locally, processed in memory, and the compressed output is downloaded directly to your device without any server involvement.

pdf-compress.q: Can I choose the compression level?
pdf-compress.a: The tool applies a balanced compression preset optimized for a good quality-to-size ratio for general use. If you need fine-grained control over image quality settings, consider using desktop tools like Ghostscript or Adobe Acrobat, which expose individual image compression parameters.

pdf-compress.q: Why is my compressed PDF not much smaller than the original?
pdf-compress.a: If the original PDF was already compressed, created from vector graphics, or contains mostly text, there is limited additional compression possible. PDFs that were previously exported from professional tools like InDesign or Illustrator often already apply compression during export. In those cases, the tool may achieve only minimal further reduction.

pdf-encrypt.q: What encryption standard is used to password-protect the PDF?
pdf-encrypt.a: The tool applies AES-256 encryption, which is the same standard used by governments, financial institutions, and security software worldwide. AES-256 is considered computationally infeasible to break with current technology when combined with a strong password.

pdf-encrypt.q: Is my PDF or password sent to a server during encryption?
pdf-encrypt.a: No. Both your PDF file and the password you enter are processed entirely within your browser. The encryption operation is performed locally in memory, and the encrypted PDF is downloaded directly to your device. Neither the file content nor the password ever leaves your machine.

pdf-encrypt.q: What happens if I forget the password after encrypting?
pdf-encrypt.a: This tool cannot recover or remove a password that you do not know. AES-256 encryption is designed to be unbreakable without the correct password. Store your password in a trusted password manager immediately after encrypting the document to prevent permanent loss of access.

pdf-encrypt.q: Will the encrypted PDF open on all PDF readers?
pdf-encrypt.a: AES-256 encrypted PDFs are supported by all major PDF readers including Adobe Acrobat Reader, Foxit, macOS Preview, and most mobile PDF apps. Older PDF readers that predate PDF 1.6 may not support AES-256, but these are exceedingly rare in modern usage.

pdf-encrypt.q: Does the tool set both open and permissions passwords?
pdf-encrypt.a: The tool sets an open password that must be entered to view the document. It does not separately configure printing or editing restriction passwords, which are a different PDF security feature. For documents requiring both open and permissions restrictions, use a full-featured PDF editor like Adobe Acrobat.

pdf-decrypt.q: Can this tool crack or guess an unknown PDF password?
pdf-decrypt.a: No. The tool requires you to provide the correct open password. It uses that password to decrypt the document — it does not perform brute-force attacks or dictionary attacks against unknown passwords. If you do not know the password, this tool cannot help.

pdf-decrypt.q: Is my PDF password transmitted to a server during decryption?
pdf-decrypt.a: No. Both the PDF file and the password are processed locally in your browser. Decryption happens entirely in browser memory, and the unlocked file is downloaded directly to your device without any data leaving your machine.

pdf-decrypt.q: What encryption types does the tool support removing?
pdf-decrypt.a: The tool supports removing standard open-password encryption used by the vast majority of PDF-generating applications, including RC4 40-bit, RC4 128-bit, and AES-128 and AES-256 encryption when the correct password is provided.

pdf-decrypt.q: Will removing the password affect the content or quality of the PDF?
pdf-decrypt.a: No. Decryption only removes the encryption wrapper around the document. All content, formatting, images, fonts, and embedded data inside the PDF remain completely unchanged in the decrypted output.

pdf-decrypt.q: Can I remove printing and editing restrictions without a password using this tool?
pdf-decrypt.a: No. Permission restrictions (which control printing, copying, and editing) are a separate feature from open password encryption and require the permissions password to remove. This tool only removes the open password that prevents the document from being viewed.

pdf-watermark.q: Can I customize the watermark appearance?
pdf-watermark.a: Yes. You can set the watermark text, font size, opacity level, position on the page (center, top, bottom, corners), and diagonal angle. This gives you enough flexibility to create visible draft stamps or subtle branding overlays depending on your use case.

pdf-watermark.q: Is my PDF uploaded to a server to add the watermark?
pdf-watermark.a: No. Watermark text is rendered and embedded into the PDF entirely within your browser. Your document is never transmitted to an external server, which is especially important for confidential contracts and sensitive internal documents.

pdf-watermark.q: Can recipients remove the watermark from the output PDF?
pdf-watermark.a: The watermark is embedded as a content element directly in the page stream, which makes it more difficult to remove than a simple annotation layer. However, it is not cryptographically impossible to strip — a determined user with professional PDF editing tools could potentially remove it. For legal protection, pair the watermark with PDF encryption.

pdf-watermark.q: Does the watermark appear on every page or just the first?
pdf-watermark.a: The watermark is applied to every page of the PDF, not just the first. This ensures that individual pages extracted from the document still carry the watermark label, which is essential for DRAFT or CONFIDENTIAL classification use cases.

pdf-watermark.q: What font is used for the watermark text?
pdf-watermark.a: The tool uses a standard built-in PDF font (Helvetica) for the watermark text to ensure compatibility across all PDF viewers without requiring embedded font resources. Custom font selection is not available, but Helvetica is universally legible at any size and opacity level.

pdf-to-txt.q: Can this tool extract text from scanned PDFs?
pdf-to-txt.a: No. The tool extracts text that is encoded as characters in the PDF's content stream — this is text from PDFs created by word processors, web browsers, or print-to-PDF workflows. Scanned PDFs store pages as images with no underlying text data. Scanned documents require OCR (optical character recognition) software before text extraction is possible.

pdf-to-txt.q: Is my PDF sent to a server for text extraction?
pdf-to-txt.a: No. Text extraction happens entirely in your browser. The PDF is parsed locally, the text content is extracted from the document's content streams, and the resulting TXT file is saved directly to your device without any server-side processing.

pdf-to-txt.q: Will the extracted text preserve the original formatting and layout?
pdf-to-txt.a: Plain text output does not preserve visual formatting such as columns, font styles, or table structures — it extracts text in the reading order encoded in the PDF, which may sometimes differ from the visual left-to-right, top-to-bottom order you expect. Paragraphs and line breaks are approximated based on the PDF's internal structure.

pdf-to-txt.q: Why does my extracted text contain garbled characters or symbols?
pdf-to-txt.a: Garbled output usually occurs when a PDF uses non-standard or obfuscated font encoding, or when the PDF was created with a tool that did not properly embed the character map (ToUnicode table). This is a known limitation of PDF text extraction and affects all PDF-to-text tools, not just this one.

pdf-to-txt.q: What is the maximum PDF size I can extract text from?
pdf-to-txt.a: There is no enforced file size limit, but browser memory availability sets a practical ceiling. Very large PDFs with hundreds of pages may be slow to process. For extremely large documents, consider splitting the PDF into sections first and extracting text from each part separately.

pdf-to-csv.q: What types of PDF tables does this tool work best with?
pdf-to-csv.a: The tool works best with PDFs that have clearly defined tabular structure — consistent rows and columns, uniform cell alignment, and tables that were created digitally (not scanned). PDFs generated from spreadsheet applications or database reports typically yield the cleanest CSV output.

pdf-to-csv.q: Is my PDF uploaded to a server during table extraction?
pdf-to-csv.a: No. Table detection and CSV extraction are performed entirely within your browser. Your PDF file never leaves your device, which is important when working with financial reports, proprietary data, or personal records.

pdf-to-csv.q: Can the tool extract multiple tables from a single PDF?
pdf-to-csv.a: The tool attempts to detect and extract all tables found across the document's pages. If a PDF contains multiple distinct tables, each may be exported as a separate section or sheet in the CSV output, depending on how the table boundaries are identified.

pdf-to-csv.q: Why does my CSV output have misaligned columns or merged cell content?
pdf-to-csv.a: PDFs with merged cells, multi-level column headers, or irregular cell spanning do not map cleanly to the flat row-column structure of CSV. The tool extracts text based on positional heuristics, so merged cells may appear as duplicate values or shifted columns. Minor manual cleanup in a spreadsheet application is often necessary for complex tables.

pdf-to-csv.q: Will this tool work on scanned PDF tables?
pdf-to-csv.a: No. Scanned PDFs store table content as raster images with no underlying text. The tool can only extract text-based table data that is encoded as characters in the PDF. Scanned tables require OCR processing to generate machine-readable text before CSV extraction is possible.

pdf-to-word.q: How accurately does the tool reproduce the original PDF layout in Word?
pdf-to-word.a: Layout fidelity depends heavily on the complexity of the source PDF. Simple text documents with standard headings and paragraphs convert very accurately. Complex layouts with multiple columns, sidebars, tables, or custom-positioned text boxes will be approximated and may require manual adjustment in Word after conversion.

pdf-to-word.q: Is my PDF sent to a server during conversion to Word?
pdf-to-word.a: No. The conversion is performed entirely within your browser. Your PDF file is parsed and converted to DOCX format locally, and the resulting Word document is downloaded directly to your device without any file content being transmitted to an external server.

pdf-to-word.q: Will I be able to edit all the text in the converted Word document?
pdf-to-word.a: All text that was encoded as readable characters in the PDF will be fully editable in the Word output. Text that was part of embedded images or decorative graphic elements in the PDF cannot be made editable through conversion — those elements will appear as images in the DOCX.

pdf-to-word.q: Does the tool work on scanned or image-based PDFs?
pdf-to-word.a: No. The tool converts text that is encoded as characters in the PDF. Scanned PDFs consist of page images with no underlying text data, so the output would contain image placeholders rather than editable text. Run scanned PDFs through OCR software first to generate a text-layer PDF before converting to Word.

pdf-to-word.q: Will fonts and styles from the PDF appear correctly in Word?
pdf-to-word.a: The tool maps PDF text styling to Word paragraph and character styles as closely as possible. However, if the PDF uses fonts that are not installed on your system, Word will substitute the closest available font, which may slightly affect line spacing and text flow. Standard fonts like Times New Roman, Arial, and Calibri are matched exactly.

word-to-pdf.q: How accurately does the tool preserve Word document formatting in the PDF?
word-to-pdf.a: The tool uses the browser's rendering engine to convert the DOCX, which produces high-fidelity output for standard Word formatting including fonts, paragraph styles, headers, footers, tables, and numbered lists. Complex elements like multi-column layouts and advanced table styles are also well-preserved in the majority of documents.

word-to-pdf.q: Is my Word document uploaded to a server during conversion?
word-to-pdf.a: No. Your .docx file is read locally by the browser, rendered using the browser's built-in layout engine, and exported as PDF entirely on your device. No file content is sent to any external server, making this tool safe for confidential contracts, HR documents, and proprietary reports.

word-to-pdf.q: What versions of .docx files are supported?
word-to-pdf.a: The tool supports standard .docx files conforming to the Open XML format specification, which covers documents created by Microsoft Word 2007 and later, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer, and other modern word processors. Legacy .doc format (Word 97-2003) is not supported — convert those to .docx first.

word-to-pdf.q: Will embedded images in my Word document appear in the PDF?
word-to-pdf.a: Yes. Images embedded in the DOCX are included in the PDF output at their inserted resolution. For the sharpest image quality in the PDF, ensure source images inserted into Word are high-resolution before converting.

word-to-pdf.q: Why does my converted PDF look different from what I see in Word on my computer?
word-to-pdf.a: Differences are usually caused by custom fonts that are installed on your computer but not available in the browser environment. When the browser cannot find the exact font, it substitutes a fallback, which can shift text and alter layout. Using common system fonts like Arial, Calibri, Times New Roman, or Georgia avoids this issue entirely.

audio-trim.q: What audio formats does the trim tool support?
audio-trim.a: The tool supports MP3, WAV, OGG, and FLAC — the four most widely used audio formats for both consumer and professional applications. These formats cover the vast majority of audio files from smartphones, recording software, digital audio workstations, and online sources.

audio-trim.q: Is my audio file uploaded to a server for trimming?
audio-trim.a: No. Audio trimming is performed entirely in your browser using FFmpeg.wasm, a WebAssembly port of the FFmpeg library that runs locally. Your audio file is processed in browser memory and the trimmed output is downloaded directly to your device without any network transmission.

For WAV and lossless formats, trimming is fully lossless. For MP3 files, FFmpeg.wasm uses stream-copy mode where possible, which avoids re-encoding and preserves the original bitrate and codec quality. The trim point will snap to the nearest audio keyframe, which may result in up to half a second of variance from the exact timestamp for MP3.

audio-trim.q: How precisely can I set the trim start and end points?
audio-trim.a: Timestamps are entered in HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS.mmm format, allowing millisecond precision. For MP3 files, actual cut precision is limited to keyframe boundaries (typically every 0.026 seconds per frame). WAV and FLAC files support exact sample-level precision due to their non-compressed frame structure.

audio-trim.q: Is there a maximum file size or duration limit for trimming?
audio-trim.a: There is no enforced size limit, but browser memory availability is the practical constraint. Very long or high-bitrate audio files (such as multi-hour WAV recordings) may require significant memory. If the browser tab becomes unresponsive, try working with a shorter segment by using the split tool first.

audio-split.q: How do I specify where to split an audio file?
audio-split.a: You provide a list of timestamps in HH:MM:SS format indicating where each split should occur. The tool divides the audio at each specified point, creating one output file per segment. For example, entering timestamps 00:05:00 and 00:12:30 splits a file into three segments: the beginning to 5 minutes, 5 to 12:30, and 12:30 to the end.

audio-split.q: Is my audio file sent to a server during splitting?
audio-split.a: No. Splitting is performed locally in your browser using FFmpeg.wasm. All audio data stays on your device throughout the operation, and each output segment is downloaded directly without any server involvement.

For MP3 files, FFmpeg.wasm uses stream-copy mode to avoid re-encoding, preserving the original codec quality. For WAV and FLAC, splitting is truly lossless with sample-accurate precision. Split points in MP3 files snap to the nearest keyframe, which introduces at most a fraction of a second of variance.

audio-split.q: What audio formats can be split?
audio-split.a: The tool supports MP3, WAV, OGG, and FLAC. Output segments are saved in the same format as the source file. If you need segments in a different format, use the Audio Convert tool after splitting.

audio-split.q: Can I split an audio file into equal-length segments automatically?
audio-split.a: The tool requires you to specify exact timestamps rather than an automatic equal-parts split. To split into equal segments, calculate the timestamps manually based on the total duration — for example, to split a 60-minute file into four equal parts, enter timestamps at 00:15:00, 00:30:00, and 00:45:00.

audio-volume.q: How much can I boost or reduce the volume?
audio-volume.a: The tool allows volume adjustment over a range suitable for correcting quiet recordings and attenuating overly loud files. Large boosts beyond the audio's dynamic headroom will cause clipping distortion, so it is recommended to boost in smaller increments and listen to the output before applying extreme values.

audio-volume.q: Is my audio file sent to a server for volume adjustment?
audio-volume.a: No. Volume processing uses the Web Audio API running entirely in your browser. Your audio file is decoded and processed locally, and the output file is downloaded directly to your device without any server transmission.

audio-volume.q: Does volume adjustment change the audio format or quality?
audio-volume.a: The tool processes audio in the browser's native format and re-encodes the output. Minor quality changes associated with re-encoding may occur, particularly for compressed formats like MP3. For lossless output, export as WAV after volume adjustment.

audio-volume.q: Can I normalize audio to a specific loudness target like -16 LUFS?
audio-volume.a: The tool provides relative volume adjustment by a specified gain amount rather than automatic loudness normalization to a specific LUFS target. For LUFS-targeted normalization, use a dedicated audio mastering tool or a DAW with a loudness meter. You can approximate normalization by measuring the current loudness with an analyzer and calculating the required gain offset manually.

audio-volume.q: Why does my audio sound distorted after boosting volume?
audio-volume.a: Distortion occurs when boosting causes audio sample values to exceed the maximum level (clipping). This typically happens when the original recording is already close to maximum volume. Reduce the boost amount, or first reduce the volume slightly below the clipping threshold before re-exporting.

audio-convert.q: What audio format conversions are supported?
audio-convert.a: The tool supports conversion between MP3, WAV, OGG, FLAC, and AAC — covering the most common audio formats for streaming, archiving, mobile playback, and professional audio workflows. You can convert in any direction between these five formats.

audio-convert.q: Is my audio file uploaded to a server for conversion?
audio-convert.a: No. Conversion is handled entirely within your browser by FFmpeg.wasm, a WebAssembly build of the FFmpeg library. Your audio file is processed locally in browser memory and the converted output is downloaded directly to your device.

audio-convert.q: Does converting between lossy formats (e.g., MP3 to AAC) reduce quality?
audio-convert.a: Yes. Converting from one lossy format to another involves decoding the compressed audio and re-encoding it, which introduces generation loss — quality that was removed by the first compression cannot be recovered. For the best quality, always convert from a lossless source (WAV or FLAC) when one is available.

audio-convert.q: Can I choose the output bitrate or quality settings?
audio-convert.a: The tool applies sensible default quality settings suitable for general use — for example, high-quality presets for MP3 and AAC output. Fine-grained bitrate control (such as specifying 128 kbps vs 320 kbps) is not available through the interface. For precise bitrate control, use the FFmpeg command-line tool directly.

audio-convert.q: Why is my converted file larger than expected?
audio-convert.a: Converting a compressed format like MP3 to a lossless format like WAV will always produce a much larger file because WAV stores uncompressed audio samples. This is expected behavior and does not mean the quality has improved — it simply means the audio is no longer compressed. Lossless formats trade file size for guaranteed preservation of all decoded audio data.

audio-merge.q: What audio formats can I merge?
audio-merge.a: The tool supports merging MP3, WAV, OGG, and FLAC files. For the cleanest merge, all source files should share the same sample rate and channel count (mono or stereo). Files with mismatched specifications will be resampled automatically during the merge process.

audio-merge.q: Is my audio uploaded to a server for merging?
audio-merge.a: No. Merging is performed entirely within your browser using FFmpeg.wasm. All source files are read locally, combined in browser memory, and the merged output is downloaded directly to your device without any file content being transmitted to a server.

audio-merge.q: How does crossfade work and what duration should I use?
audio-merge.a: Crossfade gradually fades out the end of one audio segment while fading in the start of the next, creating a smooth blend rather than an abrupt cut. For music transitions, a crossfade of 1–3 seconds sounds natural. For speech or podcast content, a 0-second crossfade (clean cut) usually sounds better than a fade blend.

audio-merge.q: Does merging files reduce audio quality?
audio-merge.a: If all source files are in the same format and specification, merging requires minimal re-encoding and quality impact is negligible. If the tool needs to resample files to match a common sample rate, a small amount of quality change is introduced. Using WAV source files eliminates this concern entirely, as WAV is lossless.

audio-merge.q: Is there a limit on how many files I can merge?
audio-merge.a: There is no enforced file count limit, but available browser memory is the practical constraint. Merging many long audio files simultaneously may slow or crash the browser tab on low-memory devices. If you encounter issues, merge files in batches of 5–10 and then merge the resulting files in a second pass.

audio-denoise.q: What types of background noise does this tool remove effectively?
audio-denoise.a: The spectral gating algorithm works best on consistent, stationary noise sources such as air conditioning hum, computer fan noise, electrical buzzing, room tone, and low-frequency rumble. These constant noises create a predictable noise floor that spectral gating can reliably suppress.

audio-denoise.q: Is my audio file sent to a server for noise removal?
audio-denoise.a: No. Denoising is processed entirely within your browser using the Web Audio API. Your audio file never leaves your device, which is important for private recordings such as interviews, therapy sessions, or confidential business meetings.

audio-denoise.q: Can this tool remove intermittent or variable background sounds like traffic or crowd noise?
audio-denoise.a: No. Spectral gating targets a stationary noise floor — sounds that change in frequency and amplitude over time, like traffic, crowd chatter, wind gusts, or intermittent clicks, cannot be reliably separated from the wanted signal. Attempting to remove these may cause musical noise artifacts or damage the audio quality of the foreground content.

audio-denoise.q: Will denoising change the quality of the voice or music in my recording?
audio-denoise.a: Correctly calibrated denoising is largely transparent to the foreground signal. However, over-aggressive settings — setting the suppression threshold too high — can cause the wanted audio to sound hollow, thin, or metallic (a phenomenon called musical noise). Start with conservative settings and increase gradually while monitoring the output.

audio-denoise.q: What audio formats does the denoise tool support?
audio-denoise.a: The tool accepts MP3, WAV, OGG, and FLAC input files. Processing is done via the Web Audio API which decodes the input to raw audio samples internally. The output is saved in a standard compatible format for immediate playback and further editing.

text-encoder.q: What encoding schemes does the text encoder support?
text-encoder.a: The tool supports Base64, Hexadecimal, Binary, URL encoding (percent-encoding), Morse code, and ASCII code conversion. These cover the most common encoding formats used in web development, network protocols, security research, and educational contexts.

text-encoder.q: Is the text I encode or decode sent to a server?
text-encoder.a: No. All encoding and decoding operations are performed entirely within your browser using JavaScript. Your input text, including sensitive strings like API keys, authentication tokens, or passwords, never leaves your device.

text-encoder.q: What is Base64 encoding used for?
text-encoder.a: Base64 encodes binary data as a string of printable ASCII characters, making it safe to transmit through systems that handle text only. It is used in email attachments (MIME), JWT tokens, embedding images in HTML/CSS via data URIs, and encoding API credentials in HTTP Basic Authentication headers.

text-encoder.q: Why does my Base64 decoded output look garbled?
text-encoder.a: Garbled output usually means the input string is not valid Base64, or it encodes binary data (such as a file) rather than readable text. Base64 strings must have a length that is a multiple of 4 — if your string is missing trailing = padding characters, add them before decoding. Also ensure the string does not contain line breaks or spaces introduced by copy-pasting.

text-encoder.q: Can I convert text through multiple encoding steps, such as Base64 of a URL-encoded string?
text-encoder.a: Yes. You can copy the output of one encoding operation and paste it as the input for another to chain multiple encoding steps. The real-time conversion updates immediately, so you can see the intermediate result at each step before applying the next encoding layer.

online-notepad.q: Where are my notes saved and are they private?
online-notepad.a: Notes are saved automatically to your browser's localStorage, which stores data locally on your device and is completely private. Notes are never transmitted to any server and are not accessible to any third party. Only the browser on the specific device where you typed them can access the saved content.

online-notepad.q: Will my notes survive if I close the browser tab?
online-notepad.a: Yes. Auto-save to localStorage writes your changes continuously as you type, so closing the tab, navigating away, or even restarting the browser will not cause note loss. Your notes will reappear when you return to the notepad in the same browser on the same device.

online-notepad.q: Does the Markdown preview support all Markdown syntax?
online-notepad.a: The preview renders standard CommonMark Markdown including headings, bold, italic, inline code, code blocks, ordered and unordered lists, blockquotes, and links. Highly extended syntax features like footnotes or custom directives may not be rendered, but all common Markdown used in documentation and note-taking is fully supported.

online-notepad.q: Can I access my notes on another device or browser?
online-notepad.a: No. localStorage is scoped to the specific browser application on the specific device where notes were created. Notes do not sync across devices or browsers automatically. To access notes on another device, export them as a TXT or PDF file and transfer the file manually.

online-notepad.q: What is the maximum amount of text the notepad can store?
online-notepad.a: Browser localStorage has a typical limit of 5 MB per origin, which is sufficient for millions of words of plain text. Extremely long documents approaching this limit may cause auto-save to fail silently. For very large documents, export to TXT periodically and clear the notepad to keep storage usage low.

json-formatter.q: Is the JSON formatter accurate for all JSON data types?
json-formatter.a: Yes, the formatter handles all standard JSON data types: strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, and objects. Numbers are preserved exactly as written, including integers, floats, and scientific notation like 1.5e10, so no precision is lost during formatting. Note that JSON does not support Infinity or NaN values — the validator will flag these as errors because they are JavaScript-specific extensions not in the JSON specification.

json-formatter.q: Does the JSON formatter handle Unicode and special characters correctly?
json-formatter.a: Yes, the formatter fully supports Unicode characters in both keys and values, including emoji, CJK characters, and right-to-left text. Special characters inside strings must be properly escaped according to the JSON spec — quotes need a backslash (\") and control characters need their escape sequences. If you see garbled output for non-ASCII characters, the input may have been double-encoded or encoded in a character set other than UTF-8.

json-formatter.q: Is it safe to paste sensitive API keys or passwords into the JSON formatter?
json-formatter.a: The formatter runs entirely in your browser — no data is sent to any server. However, as a general security practice, it is advisable to replace sensitive values with placeholder text before sharing formatted JSON with colleagues via screenshots or chat. Your browser's clipboard history may also retain copied content, so clear it after working with highly sensitive data.

json-formatter.q: Why does the formatter show an error when my JSON looks correct?
json-formatter.a: The most common hidden errors are trailing commas after the last item in an array or object (which JSON forbids but JavaScript allows), single-quoted strings instead of double-quoted strings, and unescaped control characters like tab or newline inside string values. The error position shown by the validator points to where the parser gave up, but the actual mistake is almost always in the character or line immediately before that position.

json-formatter.q: Can I use the JSON formatter to compare two JSON documents?
json-formatter.a: The formatter itself does not have a diff mode, but a useful workflow is to format both documents using the same indentation settings and then paste them into a text diff tool side by side. Formatting first normalizes key order and whitespace so the diff highlights only meaningful data differences rather than cosmetic ones. For programmatic comparison, JSON.stringify with a replacer that sorts keys produces a canonical form suitable for exact equality checks.

base64.q: Does the Base64 encoder handle Unicode and non-ASCII characters correctly?
base64.a: Yes, the tool encodes Unicode text using UTF-8 bytes before applying Base64, which is the correct and interoperable approach. Naive implementations that skip the UTF-8 step produce incorrect output for any character above ASCII 127, including accented characters, Chinese, Arabic, and emoji. If you decode Base64 from an external source and see garbled characters, the encoder may have used a different character set like Latin-1 rather than UTF-8.

base64.q: What is the difference between standard Base64 and URL-safe Base64?
base64.a: Standard Base64 uses + and / as the 62nd and 63rd characters and = for padding, all of which have special meaning in URLs and must be percent-encoded to be transmitted safely in query strings. URL-safe Base64 replaces + with - and / with _ so the output can be embedded in URLs and HTTP headers without encoding. JWT tokens and many OAuth implementations use URL-safe Base64 without padding — always check your target specification before choosing the variant.

base64.q: Is it safe to encode passwords or private keys with this Base64 tool?
base64.a: The tool processes everything client-side in your browser, so nothing is transmitted to a server. However, Base64 is an encoding scheme, not encryption — anyone who obtains the encoded string can trivially decode it back to the original value. Never treat Base64-encoded credentials as protected; use proper encryption or secrets management for storing sensitive values.

base64.q: Why does my Base64 decoded output end with unexpected padding characters?
base64.a: Base64 uses = characters to pad the output to a multiple of 4 characters, which is required by the standard. Some implementations strip padding before storage and others require it, so a mismatch causes decoding failures. If you receive a Base64 string without padding (common in JWT), you may need to add back the correct number of = characters (0, 1, or 2) before decoding — the correct count is (4 - (length % 4)) % 4.

base64.q: Can I encode binary files and images to Base64 with this tool?
base64.a: Yes, the file upload feature encodes binary file contents including images, PDFs, and archives to Base64, which is useful for creating data URIs or embedding assets in JSON configuration. The output for binary files will be much longer than text — Base64 expands data by approximately 33% compared to the original binary size. For very large files, consider whether embedding Base64 is the right approach since most image hosting and CDN solutions are more efficient.

uuid-generator.q: Are the generated UUIDs truly random and safe to use in production databases?
uuid-generator.a: Yes, the generator uses crypto.randomUUID() which draws from the browser's cryptographically secure random number generator, the same source used for TLS key generation. UUID v4 has 122 bits of randomness, making the probability of collision so infinitesimally small that it is not a practical concern even when generating millions of IDs. This is safe for production use as primary keys, correlation IDs, and session identifiers.

uuid-generator.q: What is the difference between UUID v4 and other UUID versions?
uuid-generator.a: UUID v4 is randomly generated and has no embedded information about the generating machine, time, or namespace — it is the most common choice for general-purpose unique identifiers. UUID v1 includes the machine's MAC address and current timestamp, which creates both privacy concerns and ordering properties. UUID v7, a newer standard gaining adoption, is timestamp-ordered making it more efficient for database indexes than random v4, but v4 remains the most universally supported version.

uuid-generator.q: Can I use UUIDs as primary keys in PostgreSQL and MySQL?
uuid-generator.a: Yes, both PostgreSQL (with the uuid type) and MySQL (with CHAR(36) or the binary(16) pattern for efficiency) fully support UUID primary keys. PostgreSQL's native uuid type stores UUIDs as 16 bytes rather than 36 characters, making storage and index operations more efficient than storing the hyphenated string. For MySQL, random UUIDs can cause index fragmentation due to random insertion order — consider UUID v7 or a sequential UUID strategy if write-heavy workloads are a concern.

uuid-generator.q: How do I quickly copy a generated UUID to use in my code?
uuid-generator.a: The copy button next to each generated UUID copies it to your clipboard immediately so you can paste directly into your editor or terminal. When generating in bulk, most outputs include a copy-all option that places the full list on the clipboard separated by newlines, ready to paste into a JSON array or SQL VALUES clause. In JavaScript, you can also call crypto.randomUUID() directly in the browser console or Node.js 14.17+ without needing any external library.

uuid-generator.q: Do generated UUIDs contain any personally identifiable information?
uuid-generator.a: UUID v4 is purely random and contains no information about the user, device, IP address, or time of generation — unlike UUID v1 which embeds the MAC address and creation timestamp. This makes v4 safe to expose in public URLs and API responses without leaking operational details about your infrastructure. However, the UUID itself can become a correlating identifier if linked to user accounts in your database, so treat stored UUIDs with the same access controls as other user identifiers.

timestamp-converter.q: How does the auto-detection between seconds and milliseconds work?
timestamp-converter.a: The converter uses a threshold value — timestamps above approximately 10 billion (10^10) are treated as milliseconds because that value in seconds would represent a date far beyond the year 2286, which is impractical for most real applications. Timestamps below that threshold are treated as epoch seconds. This heuristic works correctly for any date between 1970 and roughly 2286, covering the entire practical range of current software systems.

timestamp-converter.q: What timezone does the converter use for displaying dates?
timestamp-converter.a: The converter displays time in both UTC and your local browser timezone simultaneously, so you can see the server-side UTC value alongside your local equivalent without manual offset arithmetic. UTC is always unambiguous and recommended for storage and API communication, while the local time display helps you relate the timestamp to human-interpretable events. If you need to verify a specific timezone other than your local one, you can use the UTC value and apply the offset manually.

timestamp-converter.q: Can the converter handle timestamps before 1970 (negative Unix timestamps)?
timestamp-converter.a: Yes, negative Unix timestamps represent dates before January 1, 1970 00:00:00 UTC and the converter handles them correctly. A timestamp of -1 represents December 31, 1969 23:59:59 UTC. Most programming languages and databases that use Unix timestamps support negative values for historical dates, though some legacy systems and unsigned integer storage types may not.

timestamp-converter.q: Why does my timestamp convert to a date in 1970 or 2554?
timestamp-converter.a: A date near January 1970 usually means you passed a millisecond timestamp where the converter expected seconds — the value is correct but divided by 1000 gives a date very close to the epoch. A date in the year 2554 or beyond means you passed a millisecond timestamp but the tool interpreted it as seconds. Switch the input mode or divide by 1000 to correct the interpretation. Always verify the expected date range against the source system's documentation.

timestamp-converter.q: How do I convert a date and time back to a Unix timestamp?
timestamp-converter.a: Enter the date in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS) or a standard date string in the date-to-timestamp input field and the converter calculates the corresponding Unix timestamp in both seconds and milliseconds. Be explicit about timezone when converting date strings — an ambiguous local date like '2024-06-15 12:00:00' will be interpreted as your browser's local timezone, which may differ from UTC by several hours and produce an incorrect timestamp.

json-validator.q: What is the difference between strict JSON validation and JSON5/JSONC modes?
json-validator.a: Strict JSON mode follows RFC 8259 exactly: keys must be double-quoted strings, trailing commas are forbidden, and comments are not allowed. JSON5 mode accepts single-quoted strings, unquoted keys that are valid identifiers, trailing commas, and JavaScript-style // and /* */ comments. JSONC mode accepts // and /* */ comments and trailing commas but still requires double-quoted string keys, matching the format used by VS Code configuration files.

json-validator.q: Why does the validator show an error but I cannot see anything wrong?
json-validator.a: Common invisible errors include a BOM (byte order mark) at the very start of the file that looks like empty space, zero-width non-breaking space characters inside strings pasted from Word or web browsers, and Windows-style line endings (CRLF) inside string values. Another frequent issue is a duplicate key — JSON technically allows duplicate keys but many validators flag them because parsers handle them inconsistently, sometimes taking the first value and sometimes the last.

json-validator.q: Can I validate JSON against a JSON Schema with this tool?
json-validator.a: The validator checks syntactic validity (well-formed JSON) rather than semantic validity against a schema definition. To validate JSON against a JSON Schema that enforces required fields, data types, and value ranges, you would need a dedicated JSON Schema validator tool or a library like Ajv in your project.
