Some pros use aim trainers exclusively for warm-up rather than skill building, since their in-game mechanics are already well established. The consensus among professional players is that aim trainers are most valuable as a pre-session activation tool and for targeting specific mechanical weaknesses rather than as a replacement for in-game practice. Browser-based aim trainers like this one offer the advantage of quick accessibility without software installation.

cps-test.q: What is a good CPS score for gaming?
cps-test.a: The average person clicks at 6–9 CPS in a sustained effort, which is sufficient for most gaming scenarios. Competitive gaming contexts—especially Minecraft PvP—consider 10+ CPS to be above average, while highly practiced clickers using techniques like jitter clicking or butterfly clicking can reach 15–20+ CPS. For most FPS and strategy games, raw CPS matters less than click timing precision, so scores of 6–8 CPS with high consistency are more valuable than burst scores of 14 CPS that drop significantly after the first few seconds. Focus on sustainable CPS rather than maximum burst speed.

cps-test.q: What is eDPI and does it affect my CPS?
cps-test.a: eDPI (effective DPI) is your mouse DPI multiplied by your in-game sensitivity and describes your effective sensitivity—it is unrelated to your physical clicking speed measured by a CPS test. Your CPS score reflects your finger and hand mechanics, while eDPI affects crosshair movement speed. The two are independent measurements, though both contribute to overall gaming performance in different ways. If you are wondering about mouse responsiveness affecting your CPS test, ensure your mouse polling rate (ideally 1000Hz) is sufficient to register clicks accurately.

The most common techniques for increasing CPS are jitter clicking (tensing your arm muscles to create rapid involuntary clicking) and butterfly clicking (alternating two fingers on a single mouse button in rapid succession). Both techniques can significantly raise CPS scores but carry ergonomic risks if practiced excessively—jitter clicking in particular can strain wrist and forearm muscles over long sessions. For gaming rather than pure speed competition, a consistent 8–10 CPS with regular clicking technique is usually more sustainable and accurate than high-speed specialty techniques. Always listen to your body and stop if you experience any pain or discomfort.

cps-test.q: Why does my converted sensitivity still feel off after using the CPS test data?
cps-test.a: The CPS test is a standalone speed measurement tool unrelated to sensitivity conversion—if your sensitivity feels off after converting, the issue is in the conversion inputs rather than your CPS score. Sensitivity feel can be affected by mouse acceleration settings, polling rate inconsistencies, or FOV differences between games that the converter may not fully account for. Check that your mouse acceleration is disabled in Windows settings (use the Pointer Precision off setting) to ensure raw mouse input is being used correctly. Also verify that your DPI is hardware-set on your mouse rather than relying on software scaling, which can introduce inaccuracies.

cps-test.q: Do pro players train their CPS?
cps-test.a: Professional FPS players rarely focus specifically on maximizing CPS because their games rely more on aim precision and decision-making than raw click speed. However, competitive Minecraft PvP players treat CPS as a direct performance metric and actively train clicking speed as part of their skill development. For the majority of competitive games, pros focus on click timing and aim accuracy rather than maximum clicks-per-second volume. A precise, well-timed click beats a flood of inaccurate rapid clicks in virtually every FPS scenario.

reaction-test.q: What is a good reaction time for gaming?
reaction-test.a: The average human reaction time to a visual stimulus is 200–250ms, which is typical for casual gamers. Competitive gamers and esports athletes often achieve 150–180ms averages through training and consistent warm-up routines. Reaction times below 150ms are considered elite and are observed in top-level esports professionals, though genetics plays a role alongside training in determining your ceiling. Even improving from 230ms to 200ms represents a significant competitive advantage in reflex-dependent FPS scenarios.

reaction-test.q: What is eDPI and does it affect reaction time?
reaction-test.a: eDPI (effective DPI) describes your mouse sensitivity and is separate from your biological reaction time measured by this test. However, your eDPI does influence how quickly you can complete a reflex-based action after your reaction fires—a well-calibrated sensitivity means your crosshair reaches the target faster after your brain triggers the click. Reaction time is the delay between stimulus and response initiation, while eDPI affects response execution speed. Optimizing both independently gives you the full competitive advantage.

reaction-test.q: Why does my reaction time vary so much between rounds?
reaction-test.a: Reaction time variability between rounds is completely normal and reflects natural fluctuations in attention, anticipation, and motor readiness during each attempt. Factors like subconscious anticipation of the green signal, micro-movements in your clicking finger, and brief attention lapses all contribute to round-to-round variance. The 5-round average is specifically designed to smooth out this variance and give you a more representative score than any single attempt. If your variance is extremely high (50ms+ between rounds), focus on maintaining consistent mental focus and relaxed hand position throughout all five rounds.

reaction-test.q: Do pro gamers have faster reaction times than normal people?
reaction-test.a: Professional gamers do tend to have faster average reaction times than the general population, but the gap is smaller than most people assume—elite players typically average 150–180ms versus the general 200–250ms average. The more significant advantage pro players have is not pure reaction speed but their ability to predict opponent behavior through game sense, reducing the information processing step before the reaction fires. Extensive gaming experience trains pattern recognition that effectively makes decision-making faster without necessarily improving raw biological reaction time. Consistent warm-up and sleep hygiene contribute more to maintaining peak reaction time than any specific reaction-training exercise.

reaction-test.q: Can I improve my reaction time through practice?
reaction-test.a: Yes, reaction time is trainable to a meaningful degree—consistent practice can typically improve your average by 20–40ms, moving many average players from the 220–240ms range into the competitive 180–200ms range. The most effective approaches combine dedicated reaction time training (like this test) with adequate sleep, since sleep deprivation significantly degrades reaction speed. Caffeine provides a temporary 10–20ms improvement in reaction time for most people, which is why many competitive players consume it before important matches. However, genetic factors set an upper limit, and players with naturally slower reaction times can compensate significantly through superior game sense and positioning.

sensitivity-converter.q: What DPI should I use for gaming?
sensitivity-converter.a: The most common DPI settings among competitive FPS players are 400, 800, and 1600, with 800 DPI being the most widely used because it offers a balance between precision and responsiveness. The ideal DPI is ultimately the one that, when combined with your in-game sensitivity, produces a cm/360° value that feels comfortable for your mouse movement style and mousepad size. Players with smaller mousepads typically benefit from higher DPI settings, while players with large extended pads often prefer 400 or 800 DPI with proportionally lower in-game sensitivity. Avoid DPI values above 3200 for most gaming scenarios, as they can introduce hardware interpolation that reduces precision.

sensitivity-converter.q: What is eDPI and why does it matter?
sensitivity-converter.a: eDPI stands for effective DPI and is calculated by multiplying your mouse hardware DPI by your in-game sensitivity value—for example, 800 DPI at 0.5 in-game sensitivity produces an eDPI of 400. It matters because two players with completely different DPI and sensitivity combinations can have the same eDPI and therefore the same effective mouse speed, making eDPI the only apples-to-apples comparison across different hardware setups. When this converter uses cm/360° as the universal standard, it is essentially a physical-world expression of your eDPI translated through your monitor resolution and game FOV. Knowing your eDPI helps you communicate your settings clearly with other players and coaches.

sensitivity-converter.q: What is cm/360° and why is it used for conversion?
sensitivity-converter.a: cm/360° describes the physical distance you must move your mouse on the mousepad to rotate your in-game camera exactly 360 degrees, measured in centimeters. It is the universal sensitivity standard because it is completely independent of game engine, DPI, and in-game sensitivity scale—a 30 cm/360° setting in CS2 produces the exact same physical mouse sweep as 30 cm/360° in Valorant or Apex Legends. This makes it the only unit that accurately compares sensitivity across different games without requiring knowledge of each game's internal scaling factors. Professional players typically reference their sensitivity in cm/360° rather than raw in-game values for this reason.

sensitivity-converter.q: Why does my converted sensitivity still feel off after conversion?
sensitivity-converter.a: Even a mathematically perfect conversion can feel slightly different between games due to factors like FOV differences (wider FOV makes the same cm/360° feel faster), rendering framerate, input lag, and differing levels of mouse acceleration or smoothing applied by each game engine. Additionally, your mouse's sensor behavior at different speeds may produce slightly different tracking on different surfaces, which can subtly affect feel perception. If the converted sensitivity feels close but not quite right, make small incremental adjustments of 5–10% up or down from the converted value rather than large changes. After a few sessions, your feel perception often adjusts and confirms whether the conversion was accurate.

sensitivity-converter.q: Do pro players use high or low sensitivity?
sensitivity-converter.a: Professional FPS players overwhelmingly prefer lower sensitivity settings (higher cm/360° values) compared to what casual players typically use—most top CS2 and Valorant pros play between 25–45 cm/360°, which requires sweeping the mouse 25–45 centimeters for a full rotation. Lower sensitivity rewards precise, deliberate mouse movements and is especially suited for games where consistent crosshair placement and controlled tracking matter more than frantic 360° spins. However, the right sensitivity is ultimately personal—some elite players like shroud and other professionals have historically used relatively higher sensitivity and excelled. Start at a cm/360° value similar to what pros in your main game use and adjust from there based on your own movement style.

valorant-sensitivity-converter.q: What DPI do pro Valorant players use?
valorant-sensitivity-converter.a: Most professional Valorant players use DPI settings between 400 and 1600, with 800 DPI being the most prevalent on the competitive scene. Players like TenZ have used 1600 DPI with a very low in-game sensitivity to achieve their target eDPI, while others like Shroud favor 450 DPI with a moderate in-game multiplier. The specific DPI matters less than the resulting cm/360° value, which for most Valorant pros falls between 25–45 cm/360°. Use this converter to match their cm/360° range rather than trying to copy their exact DPI and in-game sensitivity combination.

valorant-sensitivity-converter.q: What is eDPI in Valorant and how do I calculate it?
valorant-sensitivity-converter.a: In Valorant, eDPI is your mouse DPI multiplied by your Valorant in-game sensitivity setting. For example, 800 DPI combined with a Valorant sensitivity of 0.35 produces an eDPI of 280. This number represents your effective sensitivity and can be compared across players regardless of their DPI hardware setup. Most competitive Valorant players have eDPI values between 200 and 400, with lower eDPI favored for rifles and higher eDPI offering slightly faster reaction potential for aggressive playstyles.

valorant-sensitivity-converter.q: What is cm/360° and how does it apply to Valorant?
valorant-sensitivity-converter.a: cm/360° in Valorant describes the distance your physical mouse must travel on your mousepad to rotate your Valorant character's view exactly 360 degrees in-game. This converter uses this measurement because Valorant's sensitivity scale (0.01–10.0) means nothing in isolation without knowing the DPI behind it, but a cm/360° value is universally meaningful. For Valorant specifically, the converter accounts for the game's FOV when calculating your cm/360° equivalent. A lower cm/360° means higher effective sensitivity—you cover more in-game degrees per centimeter of mouse movement.

valorant-sensitivity-converter.q: Why does my converted Valorant sensitivity still feel slightly off?
valorant-sensitivity-converter.a: Valorant uses a specific FOV that may differ from your source game, and if the converter does not perfectly account for each game's exact FOV implementation, a small feel discrepancy can result even with mathematically correct cm/360° values. Additionally, Valorant applies specific smoothing and input handling in its engine that can subtly change how sensitivity feels compared to games with raw input. If your conversion feels close but not quite right, adjust by 5–10% increments and give yourself several play sessions before fine-tuning further—feel perception adapts over time. Ensure mouse acceleration is disabled both in Windows and in Valorant's settings for the most reliable conversion results.

valorant-sensitivity-converter.q: Do pro Valorant players use high or low sensitivity?
valorant-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional Valorant players predominantly favor lower sensitivity settings, with most pros playing between 25–45 cm/360°, which is considered the competitive sweet spot for Valorant's precise tapping and counter-strafing mechanics. Lower sensitivity enables more consistent micro-adjustments for long-range rifle shots and precise angle holding, which are crucial skills in Valorant's tactical gameplay. Some aggressive entry-fraggers use slightly higher sensitivity (lower cm/360°) to enable faster reactive aim during close-range gunfights. If you are calibrating your sensitivity for competitive ranked play, starting within the 30–40 cm/360° range and adjusting from there based on your own feel is a solid approach.

cs2-sensitivity-converter.q: What DPI do pro CS2 players use?
cs2-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional CS2 players are heavily concentrated around 400 and 800 DPI, a tradition carried over from CS:GO where lower DPI with lower in-game sensitivity was the established competitive norm. Players like s1mple have famously used 400 DPI, while others like NiKo use 400 DPI combined with a moderate sensitivity for their target cm/360°. The CS2 professional meta strongly favors lower sensitivity overall—most pros play between 30–50 cm/360°, requiring large, controlled mouse movements. Copying a pro's DPI without matching their in-game sensitivity will not replicate their feel; use this converter to match cm/360° instead.

CS2 eDPI is calculated by multiplying your mouse hardware DPI by your CS2 sensitivity value—a player using 800 DPI at 1.5 in-game sensitivity has an eDPI of 1200. In CS2, the majority of competitive players keep their eDPI between 800 and 1200, reflecting the game's preference for lower sensitivity to support controlled spray patterns and precise rifle tapping. eDPI is a useful number for comparing sensitivity across players since two people with different DPI but the same eDPI will experience identical effective mouse speed. This converter translates your eDPI from another game into the correct CS2 sensitivity value for your specific DPI.

In CS2, cm/360° is the centimeters of physical mouse travel required to perform a full 360-degree turn in-game, and it is calculated from your DPI and in-game sensitivity. CS2 uses a purely linear sensitivity scale with no FOV modifier, making it one of the simpler games to calculate cm/360° for compared to games with FOV scaling. Most competitive CS2 players use 30–50 cm/360°, translating to relatively large, deliberate mouse movements suited to the game's precise gunplay mechanics. Using cm/360° to set your CS2 sensitivity ensures your converted value will feel correct regardless of what DPI hardware you are using.

cs2-sensitivity-converter.q: Why does my converted CS2 sensitivity feel slightly different from CS:GO?
cs2-sensitivity-converter.a: While CS2 inherited CS:GO's linear sensitivity scale, some players reported subtle feel differences after the CS:GO to CS2 transition due to changes in the game engine's input handling, rendering pipeline, and potentially subtle differences in raw input implementation. These engine-level differences can create a perception mismatch even when the mathematical sensitivity value is identical. If your CS2 feel differs slightly from your CS:GO feel despite the same settings, try adjusting your CS2 sensitivity by 5–10% in either direction and playing for several sessions before settling. Ensuring raw input is enabled in CS2 settings and that mouse acceleration is fully disabled in both Windows and the game is the essential first troubleshooting step.

cs2-sensitivity-converter.q: Do pro CS2 players use high or low sensitivity?
cs2-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional CS2 players use almost exclusively low sensitivity settings—the large majority of pros play between 30–50 cm/360°, making CS2 one of the lowest-sensitivity competitive FPS games at the professional level. This preference for low sensitivity is driven by CS2's spray control mechanics, where rifle patterns require precise horizontal and vertical mouse corrections that are significantly easier to execute accurately with larger, more controlled movements. Very few top-level CS2 professionals use cm/360° values below 25 or above 55, with the majority clustering tightly around 35–45 cm/360°. If you are grinding CS2 ranked play, calibrating within this range and focusing on spray control practice is a proven approach.

apex-sensitivity-converter.q: What DPI do pro Apex Legends players use?
apex-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional Apex Legends players most commonly use 800 DPI, though 400 and 1600 DPI setups are also represented at the top level. The Apex competitive scene has players with a wider range of sensitivity preferences than CS2 due to the game's movement diversity—tracking fast-moving legends requires slightly different calibration than precision tapping in a tactical shooter. Most Apex pros play between 25–45 cm/360°, similar to other competitive FPS titles. Use this converter to target that cm/360° range at your preferred DPI rather than trying to match a pro's specific in-game number directly.

apex-sensitivity-converter.q: What is eDPI in Apex Legends?
apex-sensitivity-converter.a: Apex Legends eDPI is your mouse DPI multiplied by your Apex in-game sensitivity value, giving you a single number representing your effective sensitivity regardless of hardware configuration. Apex's default 110° FOV affects how sensitive the game feels at any given eDPI—the wider field of view makes equivalent eDPI values feel slightly faster than in narrow-FOV games, which is why this converter accounts for Apex's FOV in its calculation. Competitive Apex players typically have eDPI values that translate to the 25–45 cm/360° range after FOV adjustment. Knowing your eDPI also helps when discussing settings with teammates or coaches.

apex-sensitivity-converter.q: What is cm/360° and how does Apex's FOV affect it?
apex-sensitivity-converter.a: cm/360° is the physical mouse distance needed for a full 360-degree in-game rotation, and Apex Legends' default 110° FOV directly influences how this converts from raw sensitivity values. Because Apex uses a wider FOV than games like CS2 or Valorant, the same cm/360° value produces a different on-screen crosshair movement speed per unit of FOV—this is why direct number comparison between Apex and narrower-FOV games requires conversion rather than simple proportion. This converter incorporates Apex's specific FOV multiplier to produce an accurate cm/360° output. If you play Apex on a custom FOV other than 110°, the feel may differ slightly from the converted value.

apex-sensitivity-converter.q: Why does my converted Apex sensitivity still feel different?
apex-sensitivity-converter.a: Beyond FOV differences, Apex Legends' unique movement system—with momentum-based movement, slide-jumping, and wall-running—creates combat scenarios where targets move in ways that may feel different from static-map games even at identical cm/360° values. The game's high time-to-kill also means tracking targets over extended durations is more common, potentially making your converted sensitivity feel slightly off until your tracking adapts to Apex's specific movement patterns. Give yourself 10–15 hours of play before fine-tuning your converted sensitivity, as your feel perception often adjusts during early sessions. Also verify you are using Apex's raw input setting and that Windows pointer precision is disabled.

apex-sensitivity-converter.q: Do pro Apex Legends players use high or low sensitivity?
apex-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional Apex players use a broader range of sensitivities than CS2 pros, with competitive players spanning roughly 20–50 cm/360° depending on their role and movement preferences. Aggressive players who use high-mobility legends and prioritize tracking fast targets sometimes prefer slightly higher sensitivity (lower cm/360°), while precision-focused players who prefer longer-range engagements trend toward lower sensitivity. The game's diverse movement and combat range means there is no single consensus cm/360° sweet spot the way there is in tactical shooters. Most coached Apex programs suggest starting between 30–40 cm/360° and adjusting based on your primary engagement range.

overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.q: What DPI do pro Overwatch 2 players use?
overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional OW2 players most commonly use 400 or 800 DPI, with 800 DPI being slightly more prevalent in the current competitive scene. The DPI varies significantly based on role—hitscan DPS players like Widowmaker and Soldier mains often favor lower sensitivity for precise aim, while support and tank players sometimes use slightly higher sensitivity for quicker target cycling. Most professional OW2 players fall in the 20–40 cm/360° range for their hitscan hero setup. Use this converter to establish a cm/360° target and then set your DPI and in-game sensitivity combination accordingly.

eDPI in Overwatch 2 is calculated as your mouse DPI multiplied by your OW2 in-game sensitivity value. Because OW2 uses a relative sensitivity system with its own FOV characteristics, the same eDPI in OW2 produces different physical mouse movement compared to CS2 or Valorant at the same eDPI—this is why the converter is necessary for accurate cross-game matching. Competitive OW2 players generally maintain eDPI values that translate to 20–40 cm/360° after FOV accounting. Using cm/360° as your target rather than eDPI directly is the most reliable approach when converting to or from Overwatch 2.

overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.q: What is cm/360° and why is it important for OW2?
overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.a: cm/360° is the universal sensitivity measurement representing how many centimeters of mouse movement produce a 360-degree in-game rotation, and it is particularly important in Overwatch 2 because OW2's sensitivity system uses relative scaling that does not map intuitively to other games' values. A cs2 sensitivity of 1.0 and an OW2 sensitivity of 1.0 produce completely different mouse feels despite the same number—cm/360° cuts through this confusion by expressing sensitivity in physical terms everyone can understand. Overwatch 2's specific FOV is factored into this converter's calculation to ensure the output is accurate. Setting sensitivity by cm/360° target is more reliable than trying to match numerical values directly.

overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.q: Why does my converted OW2 sensitivity feel off for some heroes?
overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.a: Overwatch 2's hero roster has varied mobility and ability timings that influence how sensitivity feels during active play—a conversion that feels perfect on Soldier: 76 may feel slightly fast or slow when playing Tracer's rapid blinks or Lucio's high-speed skating. Additionally, some heroes have abilities that temporarily alter camera or movement speed, which can briefly make a well-calibrated sensitivity feel inconsistent. For hitscan heroes specifically, your converted sensitivity should feel accurate; for highly mobile heroes, you may want to experiment with minor adjustments. Setting your sensitivity based on your most-played hitscan hero is the recommended baseline approach.

overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.q: Do pro OW2 players use high or low sensitivity?
overwatch2-sensitivity-converter.a: Professional Overwatch 2 players generally favor moderate to low sensitivity settings, with most hitscan DPS specialists using 20–40 cm/360° for precise aim on heroes like Widowmaker and Ashe. Tank players, who need to track multiple targets and rotate quickly, sometimes use slightly higher sensitivity than DPS specialists. Support players vary widely based on whether their kit demands precision (Ana's scope shots) or mobility (Lucio's movement).
